2280:
When something bulges, it swells or pushes outward from a surface, forming a rounded lump or bump in a place that is normally flat, straight, or smooth. The key thing to understand is why this happens: something bulges because of pressure from the inside, or because it is packed with more than it can comfortably hold. The outward swelling is a sign of that pressure. It is not just any kind of sticking out — it is a specific, rounded pushing-outward caused by something straining from within.

Think of a backpack. If you stuff it with too many books, its sides stop being flat and start curving outward. You can see the bag struggling to hold everything inside. Those sides are now bulging. The bag is overpacked, and the pressure of what's inside is forcing the fabric outward.

This is where "bulge" is used most naturally and most often.

With clothing and containers, you might say: "He had so many coins in his trouser pocket that it bulged noticeably." Or: "The suitcase was crammed so full that its sides bulged and the zipper barely held." In both cases, the container is overfull, and the excess is physically pushing the walls or fabric outward.

With the human body, "bulge" is used in a few important ways. Muscles bulge when they contract and swell with force: "His biceps bulged as he lifted the heavy box." Veins bulge when they swell under the skin due to exertion or tension: "The veins in his neck bulged as he strained to push the car." Eyes bulge when they widen so dramatically from shock, surprise, or effort that they appear to push forward out of the face: "Her eyes bulged when she opened the bill and saw the total."

With structures, "bulge" describes something being pushed outward by an outside force: "The old retaining wall was beginning to bulge dangerously under the pressure of the wet soil behind it." Here, the wall is being pushed outward by the earth and water behind it — the same core idea of internal or behind-the-surface pressure.
Figurative Uses — When "Bulge" Describes Non-Physical Things

Because "bulge" so vividly captures the idea of being overfull and straining to contain something, it is also used figuratively. When you say "His calendar bulged with meetings," you mean his schedule is packed so full that it can barely contain everything — just like an overstuffed bag. When someone says "The report bulged with useful data," they mean the report is absolutely crammed with information, overflowing with it.

This figurative use always keeps the same emotional core: something is so full or under so much pressure that it is pushing past its normal limits.
The Feel and Tone of the Word

"Bulge" is not a neutral or gentle word. It carries a sense of strain, excess, and effort. It draws your attention to the fact that something is being pushed past its normal shape or capacity. Because of this, it is a slightly dramatic, vivid word.

When muscles bulge, it suggests great physical power and exertion. When a bag bulges, it suggests the owner has packed it far beyond what is comfortable. When eyes bulge, it suggests extreme, almost overwhelming emotion. In every case, there is something slightly out of control, something being pushed to its limit. This is why writers use "bulge" when they want a strong, physical, visual image — it makes the reader see and almost feel the strain.

Understanding how "bulge" differs from similar words will sharpen your sense of it.

To protrude simply means to stick out. A nail protrudes from a wall — it just juts outward, without any implication of pressure, fullness, or strain. "Bulge" is more specific and more dramatic than "protrude" because it always implies that something is being pushed or swelled outward by a force or fullness.

To swell means to grow bigger, often gradually and in all directions — like an ankle that swells after a sprain. "Bulge" is more directional: it refers to a specific outward push in one direction that creates a visible lump. A swollen ankle grows all around; a bag bulges in the direction it is being pushed outward.

To stick out is informal and simply means to project outward. It lacks the sense of pressure and strain that "bulge" carries. A thumb can stick out, but it does not bulge unless there is some swelling or force involved.

"Bulge" appears most often in a few specific patterns, and knowing them will help you use the word naturally.

The most common is "bulge with something," which tells you what is causing the bulging: "The shopping bags bulged with groceries." "Her eyes bulged with excitement." This pattern tells you both the action (the swelling outward) and the cause (the groceries, the excitement).

Another common pattern is "bulge out," which adds emphasis to the outward direction: "The seams of his jacket bulged out at the shoulders because it was two sizes too small." This is used when the writer wants to be extra clear about the outward direction of the movement.

You will also see "bulge under": "The tent fabric bulged under the force of the wind," meaning the pressure was coming from outside and pushing the fabric inward and then outward on the other side.
A Quick Summary to Lock It In

To bulge is to swell or push outward from a surface, forming a rounded lump, because of pressure from inside or because something is overfull. It is a vivid, slightly dramatic word that captures strain, excess, and a force pushing past normal limits. It works for physical things — bags, muscles, walls, eyes — and for abstract things, like schedules or reports that are crammed with too much. Its closest rivals are "protrude" (more neutral, no strain implied), "swell" (grows in all directions, not just outward), and "stick out" (informal, no sense of pressure). When you read or hear "bulge," picture something being pushed outward by a force it can barely contain, and you will always understand it correctly.
2281:
Before diving into each meaning, here's the one idea that ties everything together:

"Bulk" always revolves around the concept of large size, large volume, or large quantity.

If you hold onto this core idea, every meaning of the word will feel natural and connected.
Meaning 1: The Large Physical Size or Mass of Something

This is the most visual meaning. When you say something has bulk, you mean it takes up a lot of physical space — it is large, heavy, or thick in a way that is noticeable.

Think of a huge wardrobe being moved through a narrow hallway. The problem is its bulk — it is simply too big, too heavy, too space-consuming to fit easily.

Examples:

  • The bulk of the old ship made it hard to navigate through the canal.
  • He was a man of considerable bulk — tall, wide, and heavily built.
  • The sofa's bulk meant that three people had to carry it.

Key feeling of this meaning: You're talking about something's physical bigness — the sheer size and weight that makes it impressive, difficult to handle, or hard to ignore.
Meaning 2: The Majority — "The Bulk of Something"

This is the most commonly used meaning in everyday reading and conversation. Here, "the bulk of" is a phrase that simply means "the greatest part of" or "most of."

You are not talking about physical size here. You are talking about proportion — how much of something belongs to one category compared to the rest.

Think of a pie. If you cut it and one person gets 80% of it, that person has the bulk of the pie.

Examples:

  • The bulk of the students passed the exam. (= Most of the students passed.)
  • She spent the bulk of her savings on the trip. (= She spent most of her savings.)
  • The bulk of the work was done by Tuesday. (= The greater part of the work was finished.)
  • The bulk of his speech was about the economy. (= Most of his speech covered the economy.)

Key feeling of this meaning: You could almost always replace "the bulk of" with "most of" and the sentence would mean the same thing. However, "the bulk of" sounds slightly more formal and precise, and it also carries a subtle sense of weight or heaviness — like you're emphasizing just how large that majority really is.
Meaning 3: In Bulk — Large Quantities (Especially When Buying or Selling)

When goods or items are bought, sold, or stored in bulk, it means they are dealt with in very large amounts, usually without individual packaging, and often at a lower cost per unit.

Imagine a restaurant that buys rice. Instead of buying small 1 kg bags like a household would, they buy a 50 kg sack all at once. They are buying in bulk.

Examples:

  • It's cheaper to buy washing powder in bulk.
  • The factory orders its raw materials in bulk to reduce costs.
  • They shipped the grain in bulk — no boxes, no bags, just loose grain poured into the cargo hold.

Key feeling of this meaning: The emphasis is on large quantity at once, usually for economic or practical reasons. Buying in bulk saves money. Shipping in bulk saves packaging. The word suggests efficiency through sheer volume.
Meaning 4: Body Mass — Size and Muscle (Fitness Context)

In the context of the human body, bulk refers to the large physical size of a person, especially muscle mass. When someone is described as having bulk, they appear big, muscular, and physically powerful.

Examples:

  • The rugby player had impressive bulk — his arms were enormous.
  • He had the speed of a sprinter but the bulk of a weightlifter.
  • She admired his bulk, the result of years of training.

You will also hear the phrase "add bulk" or "put on bulk", meaning to build muscle and increase body mass.

  • He was eating more protein to add bulk before the competition.
  • The trainer told her to lift heavier weights if she wanted to put on bulk.

Key feeling of this meaning: This is about the body being impressively large and solid — not just fat, but powerful physical size. It carries a sense of strength and physical presence.
Meaning 5: Cargo and Goods (Specialized / Commercial Use)

In trade and shipping, bulk refers to goods that are loose and unpackaged — transported in large amounts directly, without individual containers. Think of coal, wheat, oil, or sand being poured directly into a ship's storage area.

Examples:

  • The ship was carrying bulk cargo — mostly grain and coal.
  • The port specializes in handling bulk goods.

This meaning is most common in business, logistics, and trade contexts. You are unlikely to use it in everyday conversation, but you may encounter it in articles about shipping, commerce, or manufacturing.
How to Know Which Meaning Is Being Used

Since "bulk" has multiple meanings, here's a simple way to figure out which one applies:

  • If someone is describing the physical size or heaviness of an object or person → Meaning 1 or 4
  • If the phrase is "the bulk of" followed by a noun → Meaning 2 (the majority of something)
  • If the phrase is "in bulk" → Meaning 3 (large quantities, buying/selling)
  • If the context is shipping or trade and the word is used alone → Meaning 5
Common and Important Phrases to Know

These phrases are so frequently used that you should learn them as complete units:

  • The bulk of → the greatest part of something (The bulk of the damage was in the north.)
  • In bulk → in large quantities (Buying in bulk saves money.)
  • In bulk (shipping) → loose, unpackaged goods (The wheat was transported in bulk.)
  • Add/put on bulk → build body size/muscle (He's trying to put on bulk.)
  • Sheer bulk → emphasizing how large something is (The sheer bulk of the machine was staggering.)
  • The bulk → used alone, meaning "the larger part" (The bulk remains unfinished.)

——

Here is everything pulled together simply:

Bulk as a noun has one soul — largeness. Depending on the context, it describes:

  1. The large physical size or mass of an object or person.
  2. The majority or greatest portion of something (always in the phrase "the bulk of").
  3. Large quantities of goods, typically bought, sold, or stored all at once (always in the phrase "in bulk").
  4. Muscular body mass — how physically large and solid a person is.
  5. Loose, unpackaged goods in trade and shipping.

No matter which meaning you encounter, you can always trace it back to that one simple idea: something that is large in size, amount, or quantity. That's the heart of the word.
2282:
A bulkhead is a strong dividing wall built inside a structure — such as a ship, aircraft, spacecraft, or even a tunnel — to separate one section from another. It is not an outer wall; it is an interior partition that cuts through the inside of the structure, dividing it into distinct compartments.

Think of it like this: imagine slicing a submarine lengthwise and looking at the cross-section. You would see several separate rooms or sections. The walls separating those sections from each other — those are bulkheads.

The word "bulkhead" is most strongly associated with ships and submarines, and understanding it in this setting will give you the deepest understanding of the word.

Inside a ship, the interior is divided into multiple sealed compartments by bulkheads. These walls run from one side of the ship to the other (or from the floor to the ceiling), creating watertight rooms. This design is critical for safety: if one part of the ship is damaged and water starts rushing in, the bulkheads contain that water within that single compartment. They prevent it from spreading through the entire vessel. The rest of the ship stays dry and structurally sound, which keeps the ship afloat even after serious damage.

This is why bulkheads are not just any ordinary walls — they are purpose-built, engineered, structurally strong, and often completely sealed. A watertight bulkhead has special doors and seals to ensure no water can pass through at all.

Ships also have a special collision bulkhead (also called the "collision bulkhead" or "forepeak bulkhead"). This is located right at the very front of the ship, near the bow. Its job is to absorb and contain damage if the ship collides with something — so even a severe impact at the bow does not flood the entire vessel.

In airplanes, bulkheads serve a different but related purpose. The cabin of an aircraft is pressurized — meaning the air inside is kept at a comfortable pressure even when flying at high altitude where outside air pressure is extremely low. Bulkheads in aircraft help maintain this pressurization by acting as sealed structural walls at the ends of the pressurized section of the fuselage (the main body of the plane). They also divide the aircraft's body into structural zones, giving the entire airframe strength and rigidity.

In spacecraft, bulkheads similarly divide the interior and help manage the very different pressures and structural forces acting on the vehicle.

On land, "bulkhead" can refer to a retaining wall or barrier built to hold back water, earth, or other materials. For example, a concrete or wooden wall built along a waterfront to stop the land from eroding into the sea is called a bulkhead (or a seawall — the terms overlap here). In underground mines and tunnels, a bulkhead is a sealed barrier constructed to hold back floodwater or dangerous gases, protecting workers further inside.

In British English especially, the firewall of a car — the metal partition between the engine compartment and the passenger cabin — is commonly called a bulkhead. It protects the passengers from engine heat, fumes, noise, and crucially, from fire spreading into the cabin in case of an engine fire.
What Makes a Bulkhead Different from an Ordinary Wall

An ordinary wall simply separates two spaces. A bulkhead does more than that — it has a structural or safety-critical function. Bulkheads are designed to:

  • Contain something dangerous or destructive — water, fire, gas, pressure differences.
  • Provide structural strength to the vessel or structure they are part of.
  • Withstand force — whether from water pressure, air pressure, explosion, or collision.

A bulkhead is built into the structure as an integral part of it, not added on as an afterthought. This is why the word carries a sense of robustness and intentional engineering.

Because of its core meaning, "bulkhead" is sometimes used figuratively to describe anything that acts as a firm barrier separating two things — especially when the purpose is to prevent something harmful from spreading. For example, someone might say a legal clause acts as a "bulkhead" preventing liability from crossing from one party to another. This use is less common but logical once you understand the literal meaning.

A bulkhead is a strong, structurally integral dividing wall inside a vessel, vehicle, or structure, whose purpose is to separate compartments and — most importantly — to contain, block, or protect against the spread of water, fire, pressure, or damage. The word comes most naturally from the world of ships, but extends to aircraft, spacecraft, automobiles, mines, and construction. Whenever you encounter this word, the key ideas to keep in mind are: interior wall, structural strength, and containment for safety.
2283:
Something is bulky when it is large in size and takes up a lot of space in a way that makes it difficult or inconvenient to carry, move, store, or handle.

The single most important thing to understand is this: "bulky" is not just about being big. It is about being big in a troublesome, space-consuming way. When you call something bulky, you are almost always suggesting that its size creates some kind of inconvenience.
How It Differs from Just "Big" or "Large"

This is a very important distinction, and most learners miss it.

A large object is simply one that has a greater-than-normal size. That's it. No extra meaning.

A bulky object is large and awkward and takes up more space than you'd like. There is a feeling of "this is in the way" or "this is hard to deal with" built right into the word.

Think of it this way:

  • A large flat-screen TV mounted on a wall is large, but it is not particularly bulky because it sits flat and doesn't intrude into your space.
  • An old box-shaped TV from the 1990s is bulky because it sticks out far, takes up enormous desk space, and is a nightmare to move.

Same idea with a suitcase:

  • A slim, flat travel bag is large if it is wide, but it is not bulky.
  • A giant, puffed-up, hard-shell suitcase that barely fits in an overhead compartment and bumps into everyone in the aisle — that is bulky.

The key feeling the word gives you is: "This thing is too big and takes up too much room."
Bulky Things Are Often Heavy — But Not Always

Here is another nuance worth knowing. Bulky does not mean heavy. It means large and space-consuming. However, in real life, bulky things often are heavy too, which is why the two ideas get linked in people's minds.

A large, empty cardboard box is bulky — it is awkward, takes up a lot of space, and is hard to carry through a door — but it weighs almost nothing.

A small, dense block of lead is heavy but not bulky at all. It fits in your pocket.

So remember: bulky = large and awkward in size. Heavy = great in weight. They are different things, though they often appear together.

This is the most common use. Any object that is oversized, hard to fit somewhere, or difficult to move or transport can be called bulky.

  • Bulky furniture — a giant sofa that barely fits through the front door.
  • A bulky package — a box wrapped in so much material that it takes up the entire back seat of a car.
  • Bulky equipment — heavy machinery or large tools that need a truck to transport.
  • A bulky appliance — an old washing machine that dominates the entire laundry room.

You will often hear "bulky item" or "bulky goods" in the context of moving, shipping, or storage, referring to things that are too large to handle easily.

Clothing is described as bulky when it is thick, heavy, and adds a lot of volume to your body — making you look or feel bigger than you are, and often making it hard to move freely.

  • A bulky winter coat — so thick and padded that you feel like you're wearing a sleeping bag.
  • A bulky sweater — a very thick, chunky-knit sweater that adds a lot of visual size.
  • Bulky sports gear — a football player's shoulder pads, helmet, and uniform, which make them look enormous.

In fashion and clothing contexts, bulky often carries a mildly negative tone — bulky clothes are generally seen as unflattering because they hide the body's shape under a lot of fabric and padding.

When used to describe a person, bulky means they have a large, heavy, and solid physical build. It suggests someone who looks physically imposing — wide, muscular, or heavily set.

  • "Two bulky security guards stood at the entrance."
  • "He had a bulky frame that made the chair look too small for him."

Unlike the other uses, this one is more neutral — sometimes even a compliment (suggesting strength and power). A bodybuilder or a rugby player might be called bulky in an admiring way, or simply as a factual physical description. Context decides whether it's flattering or not.

In nearly all contexts involving objects and clothing, "bulky" carries a slightly negative or inconvenient feeling. You are not praising something for being bulky. You are pointing out that its size is a problem or an obstacle.

With people, as noted above, it is more neutral or even positive.

Like most adjectives, bulky can be compared:

  • The winter coat is bulkier than the spring jacket.
  • That wardrobe is the bulkiest piece of furniture in the house.

You can also soften or intensify it:

  • "The laptop bag is a little bulky but manageable."
  • "The old desktop computer was incredibly bulky compared to today's machines."

Bulky means: large in a way that is awkward, space-consuming, and inconvenient. It is not just about size — it is about size that causes a problem. It applies most naturally to objects, packages, furniture, clothing, and (more neutrally) people's physiques. The core feeling the word gives is: "This takes up too much space and is difficult to deal with because of it."
2284:
A bulldozer. It is a massive, heavy vehicle with a wide, flat metal blade at the front. It moves forward slowly but with enormous, unstoppable force. It does not go around things. It does not ask things to move. It simply pushes them — trees, rocks, buildings, mounds of earth — out of the way, crushing and flattening everything in its path.

Now hold that image in your mind. The verb bulldoze is built entirely on that image.

When "bulldoze" is used literally, it means to use a bulldozer to clear, flatten, or destroy something.

"They bulldozed the old factory to make space for a new park."
"The workers bulldozed the hillside to build a road."

Here, something that existed — a building, a forest, a structure — is pushed down and removed by brute machine force.
The figurative meanings (where the word really lives)

This is where "bulldoze" gets interesting and powerful, because most of the time you will see it used figuratively — to describe people and situations, not machines.

The figurative meanings all carry the same core feeling as the machine: massive, forceful, unstoppable pushing — with zero care for what gets crushed.

1. To push something forward by force, ignoring all opposition

When a person, a group, or an organisation bulldozes a plan, a decision, or a law, they force it through despite resistance, objections, or proper process. They do not consult. They do not negotiate. They simply push it through.

"The government bulldozed the new tax policy through parliament without any real debate."
"The manager bulldozed his ideas through the meeting, refusing to hear anyone else's suggestions."

The feeling here: something was done too fast, too forcefully, and without respect for the people or processes that should have been part of it.

2. To intimidate, pressure, or bully a person into doing something

When someone bulldozes a person, they use pressure, force, aggression, or sheer dominance to make that person do something they may not want to do. The person feels they have no real choice.

"She felt bulldozed into signing the contract before she had time to read it properly."
"He has a way of bulldozing people into agreeing with him — you leave the room wondering how it happened."

Notice the phrase "bulldoze someone into [doing something]" — this is one of the most common ways the word is used. The person being bulldozed is like the building in front of the machine: they get pushed over.

3. To move through, over, or past something with overwhelming force

Sometimes "bulldoze" is used to describe someone physically or figuratively charging through something — a crowd, a defence, opposition — with brute power and no finesse.

"The rugby player bulldozed through the defence to score."
"She bulldozed her way to the front of the crowd."
The tone and feeling of the word

This is critical. "Bulldoze" is almost never a neutral or positive word. It carries a negative charge. It implies:

  • Lack of care — for others' feelings, rights, or opinions
  • Lack of subtlety — pure force instead of thought
  • Arrogance or aggression — the bulldozer does not consider what it destroys
  • Unfairness — something (a process, a person, an objection) deserved more respect but was steamrolled

When you describe someone as bulldozing, you are criticising them — or at minimum, pointing out that their approach was excessively forceful and disrespectful of resistance.

Common structures:

  • bulldoze + object → They bulldozed the building / the deal / the opposition.
  • bulldoze + someone + into + [verb]-ing → He bulldozed her into accepting the offer.
  • bulldoze + through / over / past → She bulldozed through every objection.
  • bulldoze + one's way → He bulldozed his way to the top.
How it differs from similar words

• Push — much gentler and neutral. Bulldoze implies extreme, crushing force.
  • Force — close in meaning, but bulldoze adds the image of something being flattened or destroyed in the process, and suggests no subtlety whatsoever.
  • Bully — when used on a person, bulldoze is close to bully, but bulldoze focuses more on the act of forcing through a specific outcome, while bully is more about a pattern of behaviour.
  • Steamroll — almost identical in figurative meaning. Steamroll (from a steam roller machine) and bulldoze are near-synonyms in figurative use, and you can often swap one for the other.
One sentence to remember it all

To bulldoze means to push forward with such overwhelming, brute force — whether through a physical obstacle, a person's will, or a process — that anything in the way gets crushed or swept aside, with no care for the damage left behind.
2285: A bulldozer is a massive, extremely powerful machine used in construction and earthmoving work. Its entire purpose is to push things out of the way using brute force — soil, rocks, rubble, trees, sand, debris, or even entire structures. Think of it as a muscle machine: it doesn't dig deep into the ground the way a shovel does, and it doesn't lift and carry things the way a crane does. It simply shoves things forward, in a straight, unstoppable line.

A bulldozer has two main parts you'll notice immediately:

1. The body (the machine itself)
The bulldozer is a large, heavy vehicle that sits very low to the ground. It is built like a tank — solid, thick, and squat. It does not run on rubber tires. Instead, it moves on crawler tracks: wide, flat metal bands (like a belt) that wrap around a set of wheels on both sides of the machine. These tracks are in direct contact with the ground at all times, spreading the machine's enormous weight across a larger surface area. This is what allows a bulldozer to operate on soft, muddy, or uneven ground without sinking or slipping — something rubber tires would fail at entirely.

2. The blade
Attached to the very front of the bulldozer is its signature feature: a large, wide, flat metal plate called the blade (also called the dozer blade). This blade is set vertically — like a wall facing forward. It is incredibly thick and made of hardened steel. When the bulldozer drives forward, the blade makes contact with whatever is in front of it and simply pushes it along. The operator can control the blade: raise it up, lower it down, or tilt it at an angle. When lowered to the ground, the blade scrapes along the surface and pushes material ahead of it. When raised, the machine can drive over an area without disturbing it.

Some bulldozers also have a ripper at the back — a curved, claw-like attachment that drags through hard ground or rock to break it up before the blade pushes it.

Because of its crawler tracks, a bulldozer moves slowly but with immense power. Speed is not its strength — force is. The tracks grip the ground firmly, meaning the engine's power is transferred almost entirely into the push. This is why a bulldozer can move through thick clay, push over a large tree, or flatten a wall that would stop any other vehicle.

Bulldozers are used anywhere large quantities of material need to be moved, cleared, or leveled. Common uses include:

  • Clearing land: Before any construction begins, a site may be full of trees, stumps, and rocks. A bulldozer clears all of it in a fraction of the time it would take manually.
  • Leveling the ground (grading): Construction requires flat, even ground. A bulldozer smooths out humps and fills in dips by pushing soil around.
  • Building roads: Roads are carved out of natural landscape by bulldozers pushing away earth and rock.
  • Demolition: Bulldozers can push through walls and knock down smaller structures.
  • Mining: They move huge quantities of loose rock, soil, and ore.
  • Disaster cleanup: After floods, earthquakes, or storms, bulldozers clear rubble, mud, and debris from streets and buildings.

You'll find them on construction sites, mines, quarries, military operations, logging sites, and anywhere large-scale earthmoving is needed.
The Figurative Meaning (Used About a Person)

The word "bulldozer" is also used to describe a person who behaves like the machine — someone who uses force, pressure, or sheer persistence to get what they want, without caring about obstacles, objections, or other people's feelings. Just as a bulldozer machine doesn't stop for a tree or a rock, a bulldozer person doesn't stop when someone says "no," pushes over any opposition, and steamrolls through situations without sensitivity or compromise.

"Don't argue with him — he's an absolute bulldozer. He'll just keep pushing until everyone gives in."

This meaning carries a slightly negative tone. It implies the person is aggressive, overwhelming, and perhaps inconsiderate, even if they are effective.

A bulldozer is about unstoppable forward force. Whether it refers to the machine (a heavy, tracked vehicle with a massive front blade that clears and levels land) or a person (someone who forces their way through everything), the word always carries the same central idea: nothing in the path gets to stay where it is.
2286:
A bulletin is a short, official (or semi-official) piece of information — written or spoken — that announces something important, current, or urgent to an audience. The central purpose of a bulletin is to inform people quickly and clearly, without going into long detail.

Think of it this way: when something important happens and an authority figure, organization, or institution needs to tell people about it right now, the message they put out is often called a bulletin.
The Key Qualities of a Bulletin

A bulletin has three defining qualities that set it apart from other kinds of communication:

It is brief. A bulletin is never a long essay or a detailed report. It gives you the essential facts and stops there.

It is official or authoritative in tone. It comes from someone or something with credibility — a government body, a hospital, a news channel, a school, a company, or a religious institution. This gives it a sense of weight and trustworthiness.

It is timely. Bulletins are almost always about something current — something that just happened, is happening now, or is about to happen. They are not meant for old, settled news.
The Different Situations Where "Bulletin" Is Used

The word is used in several real-life contexts, and understanding each one helps you fully grasp the word.

A news bulletin is perhaps the most widely known use. When a major event breaks — a natural disaster, a political development, a crisis — a news channel or radio station interrupts its regular programming to deliver a short, urgent announcement. That announcement is a news bulletin. It's designed to reach people fast.

A medical bulletin is an official update on someone's health condition, usually a public figure. When a president, a celebrity, or a notable person is hospitalized, the hospital or their spokesperson releases a bulletin telling the public how the patient is doing — whether they are stable, improving, or in critical condition.

An organizational bulletin is a regular, periodic publication put out by a group — such as a church, a school, a professional association, or a company — to keep its members updated. A church might hand out a weekly bulletin during Sunday service listing the week's events, prayers, and announcements. A school might send home a bulletin at the start of each month with updates for parents. Here, the bulletin functions like a short newsletter.

An official government or institutional bulletin is a formal notice released by authorities — a health department, a military command, a regulatory body — that contains directives, warnings, or updates. For example, a public health department might issue a bulletin warning citizens about a disease outbreak.

You've almost certainly seen or heard of a bulletin board — a physical board (usually in a school, office, or community center) where notices, announcements, and messages are pinned for people to read. The word "board" here simply refers to the surface, but "bulletin" tells you what goes on it: short, informational notices meant for a group of people. In the modern world, the idea has moved online too — message boards and community forums on the internet are sometimes called bulletin boards or online bulletin boards.
How a Bulletin Differs from Similar Words

A report is longer, deeper, and more analytical. A bulletin just gives you the facts, fast.

A notice is a simple heads-up about something, often less urgent and less formal than a bulletin.

A newsletter is longer and more varied, covering multiple topics. A bulletin is shorter and usually focused on one key update or a tight list of announcements.

A press release is a statement sent specifically to journalists and media outlets. A bulletin, while sometimes similar, is addressed to a broader or different audience — the general public, members of an organization, citizens, etc.

A bulletin is essentially the world's way of saying: "Pay attention — here is something you need to know, delivered as quickly and clearly as possible, from a credible source." Whether it's a broadcaster interrupting a TV show, a hospital updating the public on a patient, a church listing Sunday's events, or a government warning its citizens — any short, official, timely piece of informational communication fits under the umbrella of a bulletin.
2287: "Bulletproof" describes something that cannot be broken through, defeated, or harmed — no matter how hard someone tries. To truly understand it, you need to understand both its literal and figurative sides, because both are widely used in everyday English.

Literally, "bulletproof" describes a physical material or object that is strong enough to stop a bullet from passing through it. A bullet is one of the fastest, most forceful small objects humans have created, so if something can stop a bullet, it is extraordinarily resistant to damage.

You will see this used with:

Glass — Bulletproof glass is used in banks, police cars, and the windows of armored vehicles. It looks like ordinary glass but is made of thick, layered material that absorbs a bullet's force without shattering.

Vests — A bulletproof vest is worn by police officers and soldiers. It is a piece of body armor worn over the chest that prevents a bullet from penetrating the body.

Vehicles — World leaders often travel in bulletproof cars, which have reinforced doors and windows to protect the person inside.

The key feeling this word carries, even in its literal form, is total, reliable protection. Not partial protection. Not "mostly safe." Completely safe from that specific threat.
The Figurative Meaning (The More Common Use)

This is where the word truly opens up. In everyday conversation, "bulletproof" is used far more often figuratively than literally. When applied to abstract things — plans, arguments, logic, strategies, cases — it means having no weaknesses, flaws, or gaps that anyone can exploit or attack.

Think of it this way: just as a real bullet cannot pierce bulletproof glass, a criticism, a counterargument, or an attack cannot pierce a "bulletproof" idea. It is airtight. It holds up perfectly under pressure.

Here are the most common figurative uses:

A bulletproof plan means a plan that has been thought through so carefully, and every possible problem has been anticipated and handled, that it simply cannot go wrong. There is no gap in it that an opponent can find and use against you.

A bulletproof argument means a line of reasoning so logically strong and well-supported by evidence that no one can find a flaw in it. If you debate someone and they make a bulletproof argument, you cannot counter it — there is nothing to attack.

A bulletproof alibi means a person accused of something has proof of where they were at the time of the event that is so solid and verifiable that no one can disprove it. It completely clears them of suspicion.

A bulletproof case (in law) means the evidence and reasoning a lawyer has is so overwhelming that losing is nearly impossible.

A bulletproof strategy (in business, sports, or military contexts) means a strategy so well-designed that the competition or enemy cannot find a way to counter or defeat it.
The Strength and Tone of the Word

It is important to understand that "bulletproof" is a strong, absolute word. It does not mean "very good" or "difficult to break." It means essentially impossible to break or defeat. It carries a sense of total invincibility.

Because of this, using it carries weight. If you call something bulletproof, you are making a bold claim. You are saying there is genuinely no weakness in it. This also means the word is sometimes used with a slight sense of admiration or awe — as if to say, "This is so good, so solid, that I cannot find a single thing wrong with it."

Sometimes "bulletproof" is used to describe a person. When someone says a person is bulletproof, they mean that person seems completely unaffected by attacks, criticism, or setbacks. No matter what people say about them or do to them, they stay strong and their reputation or position holds. This is always figurative — it is about emotional or professional resilience, not physical invincibility.

For example: "No matter how many scandals broke out, his popularity remained bulletproof." This means his supporters stayed loyal no matter what.

The word implies that someone or something has been tested or is ready to be tested — and will survive that test. It is not just about being strong in calm conditions. It is about holding up when there is real pressure, real attack, or real danger. A bulletproof argument is not just one that sounds good when no one challenges it. It is one that survives being challenged hard, by smart people, from every angle.
"Bulletproof" means so strong, reliable, or flawless — whether physically or in terms of logic, planning, or protection — that nothing can break through it, defeat it, or find a weakness in it.
2288:
Bullion refers to precious metals — primarily gold or silver — in their raw, physical form, typically shaped into bars or ingots, and valued purely by how much they weigh and how pure they are.

Think of it this way: when you hold a gold ring, you're holding jewelry. When a bank holds a heavy, rectangular block of pure gold in its vault, that block is bullion. The difference isn't the metal — it's the form and purpose.

Bullion most commonly appears as:

  • Bars or ingots — rectangular blocks of metal, ranging from small (a few grams) to very large (the famous 400 troy-ounce gold bar you'd see in a bank vault)
  • Coins — but a specific type of coin (more on this below)
  • Rounds — disc-shaped pieces similar to coins but not issued by any government

The most iconic image associated with the word "bullion" is the classic gold bar — a dense, gleaming, brick-shaped slab of metal. That is the definitive mental picture.
The Two Things That Give Bullion Its Value

Unlike a dollar bill (which has value because a government says it does), bullion's value comes from two purely physical properties:

  1. Weight — How heavy is it? Precious metals are measured in troy ounces (slightly heavier than a regular ounce). The more metal, the more value.
  2. Purity (also called "fineness") — How pure is the metal? A bar that is 99.99% pure gold is worth more than one that is only 90% gold. Purity is expressed as a decimal or millesimal fineness — for example, "999.9 fine gold" means 99.99% pure.

These two factors — and only these two factors — determine the price of bullion. This is what makes bullion different from, say, a golden sculpture. The sculpture has artistic value; bullion has none. Bullion is valued purely as a commodity, like oil or wheat.

This is one of the most important distinctions to understand.

A regular coin (like a coin in your pocket) has a face value — the number stamped on it — and that's what it's worth for spending purposes.

A bullion coin is different. Yes, it may have a face value stamped on it (for example, the famous South African Krugerrand or the American Gold Eagle), but that number is essentially symbolic and almost always far below what the coin is actually worth. A one-ounce gold bullion coin might have "$50" stamped on it, but its real-world value tracks the market price of gold, which could be thousands of dollars.

So the key rule is: a bullion coin's value comes from its metal content, not from what's written on it.

This also means bullion coins are not collected for their rarity or beauty (that would make them numismatic coins — collector's items). They are held purely as a form of owning physical precious metal.

While gold and silver are by far the most common metals referred to when people say "bullion," the term can technically apply to other precious metals too, such as:

  • Platinum bullion
  • Palladium bullion

However, in everyday use, if someone says "bullion" without specifying, they almost always mean gold. "Gold bullion" and "silver bullion" are the phrases you'll encounter most.
Why Does Bullion Exist? Who Uses It?

Bullion serves several important real-world purposes:

1. Investment and wealth storage
Many individuals and institutions buy bullion as a way to preserve wealth. Precious metals have been considered a reliable store of value for thousands of years. When economies are unstable or currencies lose value (inflation), gold bullion in particular tends to hold or increase its value. This is why people often say gold is a "safe haven" asset.

2. Central bank reserves
Governments and central banks (like the U.S. Federal Reserve or the Bank of England) hold enormous quantities of gold bullion in their vaults as part of their national reserves. This gives their economies a foundation of tangible, universally recognized value.

3. Industrial use
Silver bullion, in particular, is purchased by industries that use silver in manufacturing — electronics, solar panels, medical equipment, and more. They buy it in bulk, in bullion form, and then use it as raw material.

4. Trade and settlement
In large-scale financial markets, bullion is used to settle trades between banks and institutions that deal in precious metals.

There is an entire global marketplace dedicated to buying and selling bullion. The most important of these is centered in London — the London Bullion Market — where enormous quantities of gold and silver are traded every day, mostly between banks, governments, and large financial institutions.

The price of bullion fluctuates daily (just like stock prices), based on global supply and demand, economic conditions, geopolitical uncertainty, currency movements, and investor sentiment.
Quick Contrast: Bullion vs. Things That Are Not Bullion

ConceptIs it bullion?Why?
A gold bar in a bank vault✅ YesPure metal, valued by weight and purity
A gold necklace❌ NoIt's jewelry — it has craftsmanship value added
An American Gold Eagle coin✅ YesValued for its gold content, not its face value
An ancient Roman gold coin❌ NoValued as a rare collectible (numismatic), not just for its metal
A silver ingot✅ YesPure silver in raw form

Bullion = precious metal (almost always gold or silver) in a raw, physical form (bars, ingots, or certain coins), where all of its value comes from its weight and purity, and nothing else.

It has no artistic value, no collectible value, no sentimental value in the financial sense — just pure, dense, measurable, universally recognized metallic value. That simplicity is precisely what makes it so powerful as a financial instrument. When the world gets complicated and uncertain, a heavy bar of 99.99% pure gold sitting in a vault needs no explanation. Its value speaks for itself.
2289:
Bullish means being optimistic, confident, and expectant of growth or success — specifically the belief that something is going to rise, improve, or get better.

Think of a bull charging forward, head up, horns raised. That image of forward momentum, power, and aggression is the spirit behind the word. When you are bullish about something, you are mentally "charging forward" with confidence. You believe things are going to go up.

1. The Financial Sense (the most common use)

This is where the word is used most heavily, and where it originated in modern usage.

In finance and investing, to be bullish means to believe that the price of something — a stock, a currency, real estate, an entire market — is going to rise. A person who is bullish on a company's stock believes its price will go up, and they are likely to buy it because of that belief.

"She is bullish on tech stocks this year — she thinks artificial intelligence will drive their prices much higher."

"The analyst remained bullish on gold even as other investors were selling."

When many investors collectively feel this way and prices actually do rise over time, we call it a bull market — a market defined by rising prices and widespread confidence. The term "bullish" is the adjective describing the attitude that drives or characterises such a market.

The opposite of bullish, in this context, is bearish — meaning you expect prices to fall. A bearish investor sells; a bullish investor buys.

Degrees of being bullish:
You can be mildly bullish (cautiously optimistic, expecting modest gains), moderately bullish, or extremely bullish (highly confident of strong growth). Phrases like "strongly bullish" or "cautiously bullish" are common.

2. The General, Everyday Sense

Outside of finance, bullish is used more broadly to mean confident, optimistic, and enthusiastic about any subject — not just markets or money.

"The coach was bullish about the team's chances in the tournament."

"The CEO was bullish on the company's expansion into new markets."

"Despite the setbacks, she remained bullish about the project's future."

In this sense, being bullish simply means you hold a positive, forward-looking view about something's potential or outcome. You expect it to succeed, grow, or improve.

This use is extremely common in business conversations, journalism, and public speaking. When a politician says they are "bullish on the country's economy," they mean they are confident it will do well. When a director says they are "bullish on a new film," they believe it will be a hit.

3. The Literal, Physical Sense (less common)

Less frequently, bullish can describe something or someone that is physically large, aggressive, powerful, or resembling a bull in manner — blunt, forceful, and charging ahead without much care for subtlety.

"He pushed his way through the crowd in a bullish manner."

"Her bullish approach to negotiations left little room for compromise."

This sense carries a slight negative tinge — it suggests someone is being too aggressive or steamroller-like. However, this usage is far less common than the financial and general optimistic senses above.
How to Know Which Sense Is Being Used

Context is everything.

  • If the conversation is about money, stocks, investments, or markets → it almost certainly means expecting prices/values to rise.
  • If the conversation is about plans, outcomes, or future prospects → it almost certainly means optimistic and confident about success.
  • If describing someone's physical behaviour or manner → it likely means aggressive, forceful, or bulldozing.

In everyday life, you will encounter the first two senses far more than the third.

Bullish is always about the future. It describes a forward-looking attitude or expectation — what someone thinks will happen, not what has already happened. You would not say "the market was bullish last decade" to describe something already completed; you'd say it was a bull market. But you can say an investor "remained bullish throughout the decade" because that refers to their ongoing attitude during that period.

Bullish does not mean certain. Being bullish is about expectation and confidence, not guaranteed outcomes. A bullish investor can still be wrong. The word describes a mindset, not a fact.

Bullish can be applied to almost any domain. You can be bullish about a country, a technology, a sport, a relationship, a business, a career — anything that has a future trajectory. This flexibility makes it a very versatile and widely-used word.

If you see or hear "bullish" and are unsure of its meaning, ask yourself: Is this person expressing confidence that something will grow, rise, or succeed? If yes, bullish is exactly the right word, and you understand it correctly.
